items.title: 13.2 Derivative as the Limit of a Difference Quotient

blocks.text: Let \(f\) be a real valued function continuous in the interval \((x, x_{1}) \subseteq D_{f}\) (domain of \(f\)). Then the difference quotient

blocks.text_alt: f of x 1 minus f of x, over x 1 minus x; expression (i)

blocks.text: represents the average rate of change in the value of \(f\) with respect to the change \(x_{1} - x\) in the value of the independent variable \(x\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Read (i) as: change in output divided by change in input. It is the slope of the secant through \((x, f(x))\) and \((x_{1}, f(x_{1}))\).
A small example of ours: for \(f(x) = x^{2}\), when \(x\) goes from \(1\) to \(3\),
\[\dfrac{f(3) - f(1)}{3 - 1} = \dfrac{9 - 1}{2} = 4\]
So on average \(f\) grows by \(4\) units for each unit of \(x\) on this interval. It is called "average" because \(f\) grows more slowly near \(1\) and faster near \(3\); \(4\) is only the overall rate.

blocks.text_alt: the limit, as x 1 tends to x, of f of x 1 minus f of x, over x 1 minus x

blocks.text: provided this limit exists, is called the instantaneous rate of change of \(f\) with respect to \(x\) and is written as \(f'(x)\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Average versus instantaneous: a bus covers \(120\) km in \(2\) hours, so its average speed is \(60\) km/h. But at one moment it may be standing at a signal (\(0\) km/h) and at another moment doing \(80\) km/h. The speed shown on the speedometer at one moment is the instantaneous rate. We get it from average rates over shorter and shorter intervals, which is exactly the limit \(x_{1} \to x\).
If \(x_{1} = x + \delta x\), i.e., \(x_{1} - x = \delta x\), then the expression (i) can be expressed as

blocks.text_alt: f of x plus delta x minus f of x, over delta x; expression (ii)
the limit, as delta x tends to 0, of f of x plus delta x minus f of x, over delta x; expression (iii)

blocks.text: provided the limit exists, is defined to be the derivative of \(f\) (or differential coefficient of \(f\)) with respect to \(x\) and is denoted by \(f'(x)\) (read as "\(f\) prime of \(x\)"). The domain of \(f'\) consists of all \(x\) for which the limit exists. If \(x \in D_{f}\) and \(f'(x)\) exists, then \(f\) is said to be differentiable at \(x\). The process of finding \(f'\) is called differentiation.

blocks.title: Remember
blocks.text:
Definition of the derivative (our summary of the paragraph above):
\[f'(x) = \lim_{\delta x \to 0} \dfrac{f(x+\delta x) - f(x)}{\delta x}\]
provided the limit exists.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why replace \(x_{1}\) by \(x + \delta x\)? Then the gap between the two inputs has its own name, \(\delta x\), and "\(x_{1}\) approaches \(x\)" becomes the simpler "\(\delta x\) approaches \(0\)". Nothing else changes: (i) and (ii) are the same fraction written in two ways.
Compare (iii) with equation (2) of 13.1: it is the same limit. So the derivative \(f'(x)\) is the slope of the tangent to the graph of \(f\) at the point \((x, f(x))\).

rows: how steep the curve is at the point
how fast \(f\) changes at that value of \(x\)
the name and symbol we use from now on
the derivative of position with respect to time
blocks.caption: One limit, several names (our summary, not in the book)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A first derivative of ours, straight from (iii), for \(f(x) = x^{2}\):
\[f(x+\delta x) - f(x) = (x+\delta x)^{2} - x^{2}\]
\[= 2x\,\delta x + \delta x^{2}\]
\[\dfrac{2x\,\delta x + \delta x^{2}}{\delta x} = 2x + \delta x\]
\[f'(x) = \lim_{\delta x \to 0}(2x + \delta x) = 2x\]
At \(x = -1\) this gives \(f'(-1) = -2\), the same slope we found for \(y = x^{2} - 2\) in Example 1 (the constant \(-2\) does not change the steepness). The full method follows in 13.3.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: When asked to "define the derivative", write all of it: the limit (iii), the words "provided the limit exists", the symbol \(f'(x)\) and the name "derivative (differential coefficient) of \(f\) with respect to \(x\)". Examiners look for the condition "provided the limit exists".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Difference quotient (i) = average rate of change = slope of a secant.
2. Its limit as \(x_{1} \to x\) (or \(\delta x \to 0\)) = instantaneous rate of change = derivative \(f'(x)\) = slope of the tangent.
3. \(f'(x)\) is read "\(f\) prime of \(x\)"; another name is the differential coefficient of \(f\).
4. \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) when \(x \in D_{f}\) and the limit exists. The domain of \(f'\) is the set of all such \(x\).
5. Finding \(f'\) is called differentiation.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reading \(f'(x)\) as "\(f\) times \(x'\)". The dash belongs to \(f\): \(f'\) is a new function, the derivative of \(f\).
2. Forgetting "provided the limit exists". The limit does not always exist; in 13.5 you will see \(f(x) = |x|\), which has no derivative at \(x = 0\).
3. Confusing the average rate (a fraction over an interval) with the instantaneous rate (a limit at one point).
